Model assumptions and limitations

This laboratory explains optical principles. It does not represent an individual eye or a specific IOL. Clinical decisions require an eye examination and the exact lens model.

What is calculated?

Scalar, paraxial Fourier optics at a fixed 550 nm wavelength, with an adjustable circular pupil. The Fourier transform of the pupil phase yields a PSF whose total energy is normalized. MTF describes optical contrast transfer across spatial frequencies, not human contrast sensitivity.

The wavefront includes defocus, regular astigmatism and a chosen spherical-aberration term. Spherical aberration is set to 0.20 μm at a 6 mm pupil and scales with the fourth power of pupil diameter. This is a teaching assumption, not a corneal measurement. Ideal Aspheric compensation can cancel that term. The offset slider displaces the correction in the equivalent pupil plane; it cannot be translated into real IOL decentration.

Toric and glasses

Ideal glasses cancel cylinder only, without a reading addition. An aligned, power-matched ideal Toric correction also cancels regular astigmatism. Rotating a matched cylinder C by angle θ leaves residual cylinder 2C|sin θ|. Rotation is an optical scenario, not a probability.

How are images generated?

The photos are AI-generated streets inspired by Petaling Jaya, not records of an identified street. Their existing imaging artifacts remain. Images are converted to linear light, convolved with the PSF, then converted back to display colour. This independent laboratory uses an assumed 8° horizontal field and a 129 × 129 convolution kernel, reporting its retained energy. Edge extension avoids artificial black borders.

PSF plots use a central crop and a fixed logarithmic scale to reveal faint structure. Displayed brightness and size are not perceived halo severity. The reading text is synthetic, not a standardized eye chart.

What is not calculated?

The model omits the complete polychromatic eye, cataract scatter, retinal disease, neuroadaptation, binocular fusion and complex real IOL designs. The main app uses a simplified three-focus PSF mixture and a separate visual halo/haze control, not a real product model. This independent laboratory handles single-focus optics only.

Checks and sources

Numerical checks cover FFT inversion, energy conservation, comparison with the analytical diffraction limit, ideal cylinder and spherical-aberration cancellation, and linear-light convolution. Numerical correctness is not clinical validation. The app has not been reviewed by an ophthalmologist.
